title: Pooling and reducing allocations
body: In hot paths, allocation pressure becomes GC time. The first fixes are simple: reuse a `StringBuilder`, presize lists and dictionaries, avoid LINQ in tight loops, avoid boxing (generic APIs instead of `object`), and use spans to slice instead of `Substring`/`ToArray`.

`ArrayPool<T>.Shared.Rent(minimumLength)` lends an array that may be longer than requested; `Return(array)` gives it back for reuse. Always track the length you actually use, never use an array after returning it, and return it in a `finally` so exceptions do not leak pool arrays. Pass `clearArray: true` when the buffer held sensitive data.

`ObjectPool<T>` (Microsoft.Extensions.ObjectPool) pools larger reusable objects; `string.Create(length, state, (span, state) => ...)` builds a string by writing into its final buffer once. `stackalloc` with a size threshold and a pool fallback is a common pattern: small buffers on the stack, large ones rented.

Measure before and after. `GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread()` in a test, BenchmarkDotNet's `[MemoryDiagnoser]` for micro-benchmarks, and `dotnet-counters` in production show whether a change actually reduced allocation. Readability costs are real; optimize the paths the measurements point at.

Pools turn memory bugs into data bugs: a returned array still in use gets overwritten by the next renter. Check every Rent has exactly one Return on every path and that nothing keeps the array afterwards.
